catalog_quote: p.15: "4. ACCENT In order to obtain a good pronunciation of these languages, especially of Ndogo, great attention must be paid to the accent. The following suggestions (I shall not call them rules) may serve as a guide for Ndogo. I. No difficulty for monosyllables. II. In connection with polysyllables, attention must be paid to the fact that a good few of such words are compound ones, actually made up of two or more monosyllables, each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed. ... III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first. The latter are listed here as a guide to the reader: words having l r n in the second syllable. E.g.: toro kátá mele ngele kele téné sènè. koro moro ... IV. In reduplicated dissyllables we find that: (a) the accent lies often on …

new_statements.quote: p.15: "The following suggestions (I shall not call them rules) may serve as a guide for Ndogo. [...] II. In connection with polysyllables, attention must be paid to the fact that a good few of such words are compound ones, actually made up of two or more monosyllables, each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed. [...] III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first." p.29: "(d) As hinted above (5. iv.), the accent usually lies on the first syllable of dissyllables: thus, in reduplication, accents lie on the first and third syllables."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under The named file contains the quoted p.15 and p.29 passages exactly as given in the report, and I re-verified each against the raw Google Books search-within-volume JSON captured via IA Save Page Now: 'The follow- ing suggestions ( I shall not call them rules) may serve as a guide for Ndogo. I. No difficulty for monosyllables. II. In connection with polysyllables.. compound ones' (p.15), '.. actually made up of two or more monosyllables, each one of which must have its own accent duly stressed' (p.15), 'III. The most noteworthy difference in accent exists among words of two syllables, some having an even stress on both syllables, and some having a real accent on the first'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndogo is described with a separate tone system (low/mid/high/very high, pp. 16-33) plus an 'accent' treated impressionistically: monosyllables unproblematic; disyllables either evenly stressed or accented on the first syllable (the usual case, especially when the second syllable contains l, r or n, whose vowel is often lost: mbòro > mbòò, kóró > kóó); polysyllables are mostly compounds in which each monosyllabic component keeps its own accent; reduplicated disyllables carry accent on the 1st and 3rd syllables. I.e. a word/stem-initial prominence tendency, explicitly offered as 'suggestions, not rules'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; in compounds each component 'must have its own accent duly stressed', and reduplications have accents on the first and third syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Some disyllables have 'an even stress on both syllables'; in reduplications 'occasionally the opposite phenomenon is met with, viz. the accent lies on the second syllable' (mbulambula / mbulàmbulà, the only exception among his examples); predicative adjectives/verbs with lengthened final vowel take 'accent on the doubled vowel' (p. 26). Remark V (on Bviri) not recovered.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level pronunciation guidance for citation forms ('to obtain a good pronunciation.. great attention must be paid to the accent'); author hedges that these are suggestions for Ndogo specifically, not rules; 'stress' on pp. 54, 145 refers to sentence emphasis, not word accent.
new_statements.identity_note: Santandrea's accent remarks are explicitly 'a guide for Ndogo' (the Ndogo of the Wau area, Bahr el Ghazal = ndog1248) within a comparative grammar that also covers Sere (sere1264), Tagbu, Bai and Bviri/Belanda Viri (bela1255); remark V on p. 15 concerns Bviri and was not recovered. Ndogo is also tonal (Santandrea sec. 5, pp. 16-33; Bilal 2004: three level tones + falling).
